in statements like: though I cannot avail you anything against Allah. Sovereignty belongs only to Allah (12:67), the warning: We apprised him of the matter that these will be rooted out by dawn (15:66), and the declaration: and when He decides on a matter, He just says to it, ‘Be!’ and it is (2:117).

God also describes His divine decree using the term ‘word’ (kalima). As noted in the Qur’an: “Indeed, Our word has already preceded for Our servants, the messengers, that they will certainly be the victors” (37:171). Additionally, it is stated: “Certainly Our decree has gone beforehand in favor of Our servants, the messengers, that they will indeed receive help” (37:172). Regarding Jesus, it is articulated: “Indeed the case of Jesus with Allah is like the case of Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him, ‘Be,’ and he was” (3:59). Furthermore, in reference to Jesus: “and His W ord that He cast toward M ary and a spirit from Him” (4:171). These diverse terms— saying, word, command, will, decree—highlight the various manifestations

of God’s act of creation, emphasizing that all is encompassed and directed by God’s sovereign command.

Drawing from these insights, it’s understood that God Almighty’s act of creation— bestowing existence upon entities, which essentially is their very existence— is encapsulated in His command (amr), His utterance (qawl), and His word (kalima). However, based on the explicit phrasing in the Qur’an, it becomes clear that God’s word is specifically manifested through His saying, characterized by its definitive and decisive nature. This elucidation reveals that God’s will (irāda) and His decree (qaḍāʾ) are unified, holding a precedence in the order of existence over His saying and command. Hence, God Almighty initially wills and decrees a matter. Subsequently, He manifests this will through His command, pronouncing ‘Be,’ and thus, it materializes into existence.

God has demonstrated that nothing can veer away from His command, asserting that His word embodies truth. As it’s stated: “It is He who created the heavens and the earth with reason, and the day He says, ‘Be!’ it is. His word is the truth” (6:73). This indicates that His word is not only truth in declaration but also in its manifestation in reality, mirroring the concrete external reality that is His act. Consequently, deviation from His will, the emergence of falsehood, or the presence of invalidity are inconceivable. It’s inherently understood that a fact of existence or an established reality is immutable. Hence, God’s acts, which are actualities, are devoid of errors or mistakes. His command remains unchallenged, His word unrefuted, and His promise invariably fulfilled.

Drawing from this verse, as well as the preceding one where the polytheists assert, ‘Had Allah wished, we would no t have worshiped anything

besides Him’ (16:35), it’s evident that two forms of divine will are ascribed to God. The first is the creative will (irādat al-takwīni), which is absolute and unchangeable. The second is the legislative will (irādat al-tashrīʿ), which is subject to human response—it can be met with either compliance or defiance. This topic will be further explored and expanded upon shortly.

Examining Narrations

(1) In Tafsīr al-Qummī, it narrated via his own chain of narration from Abū Jaʿfar, regarding the verse, Those who were before them had also schemed. Then Allah razed their edifice from the foundations and the roof collapsed upon them from above and the punishment overtook them whence they were not aware: ‘It refers to the

house of their schemes, meaning they died, and God caused them to dwell in Hellfire eternally. This is a metaphor for the enemies of the Family of Muḥammad.’

Author’s comment: The apparent meaning of this narration is that the phrase, Then Allah razed their edifice from the foundations is a metaphor for the invalidation of their schemes, not their physical homes.

(2) And in Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated from Muḥammad b.

Muslim from Abū Jaʿfar, who said: The meaning of then Allah razed their edifice from the foundations was the house where they would gather to conspire in harming and oppressing the prophets.

(3) In Tafsīr al-Qummī, concerning the phrase, Those who were given knowledge will say …, it is relayed from the Imām: ‘The intended referents of Those who were given knowledge are the Imāms who will say to their enemies: ‘W here are your partners and those whom you obeyed in the world?’ … The Imām stated: ‘Those whose souls the angels are taking while they are wronging themselves are the same group who, when calamities befall them, submit and say, ‘W e were not doing any evil!’— but God rejects their statement, saying: ‘Yes, indeed Allah knows best what you used to do!’

(4) Shaykh al-Ṭūsī narrates in his Amālī via his chain of narrators from Abū Isḥāq al-Hamadānī, who narrates from the Commander of the Faithful that, in a letter written to the people of Egypt, he said: ‘O servants of God, the moment when a servant is nearest to forgiveness and mercy is when they act in obedience to God and sincerely repent. I adjure you to observe Godwariness, for it encompasses all good, and there is no good beyond it. Through Godwariness, one attains a portion of the good of this world and the hereafter. Indeed, God Almighty has said: But to those who were Godwary it will be said, ‘W hat is it that your Lord has sent down?’ They will say, ‘Good.’ For those who do good in this world there will be a good reward, and the abode of the Hereafter is better, and the abode of the Godwary is surely excellent (16:30).

(5) In Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī, it is narrated via Ibn M iskān from Abū Jaʿfar, concerning the phrase, and the abode of the Godwary is surely excellent, it is interpreted to mean this world.

(6) And in Tafsīr al-Qummī, concerning the phrase those whom the angels take away while they are pure, it is narrated from the Imām that it refers to the believers whose birth in this world is pure.

Author’s comment: Given that the earlier phrase, Those whom the angels take away while they are wronging themselves, mirrors the verse under discussion, it does not appear that this narration yields a clear meaning. However, since the narration is weak in any case, this is not a matter of concern.

(7) In al-Durr al-Manthūr, it is reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim from al-Sudayy, who related: ‘The Quraysh gathered and said among themselves that Muḥammad is a man of sweet speech and when someone converses with him, he influences them so much that it seems as if he takes away their intellect. Therefore, they agreed to select a limited number of their nobles, who were well-known by lineage, and recognizable by strangers, and then every night, or every other night, send them to stand on the roads of Mecca to dissuade the newcomers who come to visit Muḥammad from proceeding. They carried out this plan, and each took position on a road; whenever they saw someone coming from outside M ecca, either to inquire about their relatives or to personally see Muḥammad, they would approach, introduce themselves as recognized individuals, and then say, “I inform you about the situation

with Muḥammad: he is a liar, followed only by the foolish, the senseless, a bunch of slaves, or those devoid of any good. The elders and dignitaries of his people have all turned away from him.” They would fabricate such lies to turn the person away right from the middle of the road. And the verse When they are told, ‘What is it that your Lord has sent down?’ They say, ‘Myths of the ancients,’ was revealed concerning this matter.

If such an individual, one whom God wished to guide, were to enter among the skeptics, he would respond: “We have come as ambassadors on behalf of our people, and what poor ambassadors we would be if, after traveling such a great distance — now less than a day’s journey away —we were to return without having met this man to hear what he has to say, so we could convey his message to our people. No, this cannot be; we must see this man and speak with him, then bring his news back to our people.” And this they did. Upon entering the city of Mecca, they would meet with the followers of that esteemed person and inquire, “What does Muḥammad say?” They would reply, “He speaks of goodness and gives glad tidings that for anyone who does good, there is

prosperity and a comfortable life in this world, and certainly, the home in the afterlife, which is paradise, is even better.”

Author’s comment: The story seems credible, however the latter most part, which interprets the term ‘good’ as material wealth, is unacceptable. (8) In al-Kāfī, al-Kulaynī relates via his chain of narrators from Ṣafwān b. Yaḥyā, it is narrated that he said: I asked Abū al-Ḥasan, ‘What is the difference between the will of God and the will of His creatures?’ He replied, ‘The will of creatures consists of the intention within the heart and the actions that follow it, whereas the will of God Almighty is the act of bringing into existence and creating, nothing else. For God does not think or decide, and such attributes are far removed from His sacred essence. Indeed, these are the attributes of His creations. Thus, the will of God is His act itself, nothing else. W hatever He wills, He says ‘Be,’ and it is. Moreover, even this saying is not by voice or word, nor by intention or thought, and it cannot even be described how it is, for God is beyond the ‘how.’”

(9) In al-Durr al-Manthūr, al-Suyūṭī reports that Aḥmad and Tirmidhī (who considered the chain of narration good), Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī in the book Shuʿub al-Īmān, all have transmitted from Abū Dharr, who quotes the Messenger of God as saying: ‘God Almighty says to the children of Adam: “O children of Adam, all of you are sinners except for those whom I have forgiven. Therefore, seek My forgiveness, and I shall forgive you. All of you are needy except for those whom I have enriched. Hence, ask of Me, and I shall give to you. And all of you are astray except for those whom I have guided. Thus, ask for My guidance, and I shall guide you. And whoever seeks My forgiveness, knowing that I am able to forgive, I shall forgive him and I have no reservations in doing so.

And if the first and the last, the living and the dead, the moist and the dry among you were all to gather together to maintain the most wretched among you in his wretchedness, they would not diminish My dominion or power even by the weight of a mosquito. And if I wish, I can incline him toward good. And if the first

and the last, the living and the dead, the moist and the dry among you were to unite their hearts to assist the most righteous among you, they would not increase My dominion or power even by the weight of a mosquito. Thus, your aid has no effect on the power of God. And if the first and the last, the living and the dead, the moist and the dry among you were all to ask of Me so that there would be no request left, and I were to grant the requests of all of you, it would not diminish from My vast sea of generosity even by the amount that a needle reduces from the sea when it enters the water. This is because I am Generous, Majestic, and Unique. My giving is a word and My punishment is a word. My command for something when I will it is merely to say ‘Be’, and it immediately comes into existence.’
